news_coverage.summary: Hadleigh McAlister talks about Salvation Army funding in the city budget after deliberations wrapped up Wednesday, Nov. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press) Londoners will face a 3.4 per cent property tax hike next year, a figure that includes a new addition of temporary rental assistance as part of the city budget finalized Wednesday. The funding will go toward financial assistance for low-income Londoners for rent and utilities to help them retain housing. Budget chair Elizabeth Peloza was absent. The increase won’t move the needle on next year’s now-final tax hike, which represents a $51 increase for every $100,000 in a home’s assessed property value. “No, I’m not going to veto any of the changes council made,” he said, promising a formal declaration Thursday. “I do have the ability to waive my veto period to basically no time at all, and then that essentially will end the budget process.” The 2026 budget update initially began at a forecasted 6.4 per cent tax hike at the end of last year’s talks. Right-sizing by city hall and some of its agencies, plus surplus money injected to lower taxes, contributed to the final tally. Among the biggest additions are $2.3 million to help pay off office relocation debt for the Middlesex-London Health Unit, and $784,000 to provide two free hours of on-street parking in London’s core.
